parts.note: a London rail terminus that shares its name with a famous storybook bear from Peru, so 'bearable' puns on 'able to have a bear'

explanation.surface: A grumpy commuter wonders which London terminus is actually tolerable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bearable' looks like 'tolerable', but here it means 'connected with a bear': the children's-book bear found at this station took its name.
explanation.definitionFit: The fictional bear in the duffel coat is named after the west London terminus where he was found.

parts.note: the name of the 18th-century English poet Alexander is also the title of the head of the Catholic Church in Rome

explanation.surface: A visiting writer turns up at the papal city.
explanation.walkthrough: The word serves twice: as the surname of the poet Alexander, who wrote 'The Rape of the Lock', and as the title of the pontiff who lives in the Vatican.
explanation.definitionFit: The Vatican is home to the head of the Roman Catholic Church, whose title is also an English poet's surname.

explanation.surface: Perhaps there will be a light shower.
explanation.definitionFit: A single bead of water is a tiny amount of rain, and to plunge or sink downward is the verb sense.

indicators.note: the words are taken on a tour, travelling about until their letters land in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A holiday report: the trip was ruined because it rained far too much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Toured' looks like the start of a travel story, but it is the anagram signal on ONLY IT RAINED.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something beyond reasonable limits is doing it to an unreasonable degree, an adverb like the clue word.

clue.text: American girl may cut and run

parts.note: gal is a colloquial, especially American, word for a girl
to lop is to cut off, as branches from a tree

explanation.surface: An American woman might slash something and then flee.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse's fastest pace is a run, and to go at that pace is to race along.

clue.text: From patch of gorse I'll extract lichen

indicators.note: the letters come from a stretch, or patch, of the following words, sitting within them

explanation.surface: A naturalist draws lichen out of a clump of gorse.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits inside gORSE I'LL Extract, ignoring the apostrophe.
explanation.definitionFit: A purple dye, also called archil, made from certain lichens, and by extension the lichen itself.

parts.note: love is zero in tennis scoring, which looks like the letter O
a pen is an instrument for writing

explanation.surface: Someone is at liberty to adore an author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' suggests an author, but here it is the tool that does the writing.
explanation.definitionFit: Something not closed or restricted is unrestricted, available to all.

clue.text: Spoils peer looted from ancient capital

indicators.note: something looted has been ransacked and thrown about, so these letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A nobleman carries off treasure plundered from an old seat of empire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoils' and 'looted' read as one plunder story, but the two words SPOILS PEER are the anagram fodder and 'looted' its signal.
explanation.definitionFit: This was the ceremonial seat of the Persian Achaemenid kings, sacked by Alexander the Great.

clue.text: In the dark, stay up by the bedside table

parts.note: the dark hours of the day are the night
to stand is to stay upright on your feet

explanation.surface: Someone stays up late at night beside a little bedroom table.
explanation.definitionFit: A small table kept by a bed, chiefly an American term, is the same piece of furniture.

clue.text: First psalm, translated, provides the basis for life

parts.note: proto- is a combining form meaning first or earliest

indicators.note: something translated has been turned into another form, so the letters of psalm are rearranged

explanation.surface: Rendering the opening psalm into another language reveals the foundation of existence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First psalm' looks like a reference to Psalm 1, but 'First' gives PROTO and 'translated' turns PSALM into PLASM.
explanation.definitionFit: The living substance of a cell was long described as the physical foundation of all living things.

explanation.surface: A floating jail, like the old convict hulks.
explanation.definitionFit: In navy slang a lock-up on board or ashore is so called, and the word also names a two-masted square-rigged sailing vessel.

parts.note: a vivid magenta shade whose name contains a word meaning appalling, so 'dreadful' describes the name as much as the hue

explanation.surface: Someone recoils at a garish paint shade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dreadful' seems a judgment on taste, but it hints at the first word of the colour's name, which means appalling.
explanation.definitionFit: A loud, intense magenta made fashionable by the designer Elsa Schiaparelli in the 1930s.

clue.text: Man hints dome is disastrous and gets a telling-off!

indicators.note: a disastrous state is a wrecked one, so these words are knocked into a new letter order

explanation.surface: Someone is scolded because their suggestions for a dome are a catastrophe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is disastrous' reads as a verdict on the dome; 'disastrous' is the anagram signal on MAN HINTS DOME.
explanation.definitionFit: A reprimand or scolding is a formal warning given for bad conduct.

clue.text: People standing while seats are vacant

definitions.text: People standing while seats are vacant

parts.words: People standing while seats are vacant
parts.note: reads like passengers standing in a half-empty carriage, but means those who stand for election to fill empty parliamentary seats

explanation.surface: Commuters stand in a carriage even though there are free seats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standing' means offering oneself for election, and the vacant seats are in parliament or on a council, not on a train.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who stand for election to a vacant post are contenders for office.

clue.text: Judge gets publicity — caught with two girls, it's reported

parts.note: an ad, short for advertisement, is a piece of publicity

indicators.note: what is reported is heard spoken, so the two names are taken by their sound

parts.note: the girls' names Judy and Kate

explanation.surface: A tabloid story: a judge is exposed after being caught with two women.
explanation.walkthrough: Said together, the names Judy and Kate sound like the end of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To act as an arbiter and give a formal ruling on a dispute, a verb like the clue word.

parts.note: the Forest of Arden in Warwickshire, the setting of Shakespeare's As You Like It

indicators.note: first asks for the opening letter of the word trees, placed at the end here

explanation.surface: A forest's trees catch fire first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' says take the initial letter of 'trees', not that the trees come first in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Passionate or fervent feeling is figuratively fiery, glowing with intensity.

explanation.surface: Someone swoons when the electricity fails.
explanation.definitionFit: A temporary loss of consciousness, and also a failure of electricity supply darkening an area.

clue.text: English river name in old Italian region

parts.note: the Trent is a major river of the English Midlands

explanation.surface: An English river's name turns up in a historic Italian province.
explanation.definitionFit: An Alpine area of northern Italy, centred on the city of Trento, part of an autonomous region.

parts.note: the apostle Thomas would not believe in the Resurrection until he saw the wounds, giving the phrase 'doubting Thomas'

explanation.surface: Unbelievers such as the apostle Thomas.
explanation.definitionFit: People who question or disbelieve, as the apostle who demanded proof did.

explanation.surface: A painter's favourite shade.
explanation.definitionFit: The Venetian painter Tiziano Vecellio is known in English by this name, and it also names the bright reddish-gold hair colour he favoured.

clue.text: Stop during a run to take a breather

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run
to rest is to pause and take a breather

explanation.surface: A jogger halts mid-run for a breather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stop' looks like an instruction to the runner, but it is the definition, as in the police stopping a suspect.
explanation.definitionFit: Police detaining a suspect bring them to a halt, so the verb means to check or halt.

clue.text: Well, well, so that's what they're for!

definitions.text: Well, well, so that's what they're for!

parts.words: Well, well, so that's what they're for!
parts.note: reads as a surprised exclamation, but 'well, well' means oil or water wells, the things such apparatus bores

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in surprise at discovering the purpose of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well, well' is not mild surprise: wells are what the structures are built to bore.
explanation.definitionFit: Tall rigs used to bore boreholes for oil, gas or water.

parts.note: ti is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the cipher of Queen Elizabeth

explanation.surface: Someone takes note of the queen's position.
explanation.definitionFit: A row or level in a stepped arrangement is a grade or layer.

indicators.note: semi means half, so only the first half of the word agrarian is used

explanation.surface: A partly rural town.
explanation.walkthrough: The prefix 'semi-' takes the first four of the eight letters of 'agrarian'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Indian city in Uttar Pradesh that is home to the Taj Mahal.

parts.note: R is an abbreviation for rector; that the letters also run across the words Tea rector is a coincidence of the charade, not a hiding device

explanation.surface: A host offers the vicar tea, and he asks for only a little.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just a drop' sounds like the rector's reply about his tea, but it defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny bead of liquid shed from the eye, a teardrop.

explanation.surface: Something refreshing, the way a mother always is.
explanation.definitionFit: Something bracing restores vitality, and every mother is literally the one who bore a child.

indicators.note: the clue says outright that a word sounding the same is wanted

parts.note: a Sikh is a follower of a religion founded in the Punjab, India

explanation.surface: A request to find a word sounding like a term for someone from India.
explanation.definitionFit: To search for something is to try to find it.

clue.text: Asian country that shook a true revolutionary

indicators.note: something revolutionary turns things right over, so these letters are overturned into a new order

explanation.surface: An Asian nation rattled by a genuine rebel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' looks like a noun for a rebel, but it signals the anagram of SHOOK A TRUE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Republic of Korea occupies the southern half of the Korean peninsula in East Asia.
